passage: Siddharth set down his chai and told his cousin, "You know I take the ethics tutorial now, right? Twenty-two and grading people nearly my age. Strange. So there's this student, Pradeep. In the debate on copying assignments, he said flatly, 'Don't copy, because you'll get caught and lose marks.' Classic Kohlberg stage one, I thought, and I nearly wrote him off. Then last week we discussed a clinic that turned away a patient without papers, and Pradeep argued that laws exist to protect people and this one was failing its own purpose. That's miles further along the same ladder. Same student, same month. So I stopped treating the stages like labels stamped on foreheads. They're more like which tools someone reaches for in a particular room. My job is to build rooms where the better tools come out."

qa.q: What did Pradeep say in the debate on copying assignments?
qa.a: 'Don't copy, because you'll get caught and lose marks.'

qa.q: How did Siddharth feel after Pradeep's argument about the clinic?
qa.a: He was surprised to see the same student reason much further along the ladder in a different situation, and realised his first judgement of Pradeep had been wrong.

qa.q: What choice did Siddharth make after noticing this, and how might it help his students?
qa.a: He chose to treat the stages as tools people reach for in different rooms and to build discussions that bring out stronger reasoning, rather than labelling students.

qa.q: How might Pradeep have been affected if Siddharth had written him off after the first debate?
qa.a: Pradeep might have been treated as a shallow thinker, and his stronger reasoning about the clinic could have gone unnoticed.

grounding: A young tutor who knows Kohlberg's model sees one student reason at very different levels and treats the stages as tendencies rather than labels on people.

passage: I've shared a staffroom with Yamini at the degree college for two years, so I noticed when she started jotting notes about Vaibhav. He's the first-year who, in the ethics debate, said a shopkeeper who overcharges should be stopped "because the police will fine him." A week later, in a case about a friend asking to copy his project, he refused because "the whole class trusts the teacher to be fair, and copying breaks that." Yamini read both lines aloud to me and laughed. "Same boy, two different levels in one week." Some colleagues rank students by these stages as if they were marks. She doesn't. She told me the model is a map of how thinking can grow, not a scorecard of goodness. I can't say what she really feels about him. But she gave him the hardest case in the next debate.

qa.q: Why did Vaibhav say an overcharging shopkeeper should be stopped?
qa.a: "Because the police will fine him."

qa.q: What does Yamini's laugh suggest about how she felt reading both lines?
qa.a: She seemed delighted and curious to see the same student reason at two different levels in one week.

qa.q: What choice did Yamini make for the next debate, and why might it help Vaibhav?
qa.a: She gave him the hardest case, which invites the stronger reasoning he showed about trust instead of boxing him at the lower level.

qa.q: How does the narrator's view of Yamini's approach differ from how some colleagues use the stages?
qa.a: The narrator notices that Yamini treats the stages as a map of growth, while some colleagues rank students by them like marks, and the narrator seems to find Yamini's way worth recording.

grounding: A colleague observes a teacher notice one student reasoning at different levels and treat the stage model as a map of growth rather than a ranking of people.

passage: Monday. Deepika, in her first year teaching the college's values course, read Farida's essay on a stolen exam paper: "Don't take it, you'll be expelled." She pencilled "stage one?" in the margin and felt a little let down. Thursday. In group work, Farida argued that the hostel curfew should be changed by a student vote, because "rules are agreements, and this one ignores students who work evening shifts." Deepika stopped mid-stride between the desks. That was reasoning from a very different place. The following Monday, Deepika rubbed out the pencil note. In her planning book she wrote: "Stages describe the reasoning in a moment, not the person. Farida reaches higher when the question touches her own life." She built the next week's cases around the students' own hostels and part-time jobs.

qa.q: What did Deepika pencil in the margin of Farida's essay?
qa.a: "stage one?"

qa.q: What was Deepika feeling when she stopped mid-stride on Thursday?
qa.a: She was surprised, realising Farida could reason from a very different place than her essay suggested.

qa.q: What did Deepika change after rubbing out the note, and why is it a good choice?
qa.a: She built the next cases around the students' own hostels and part-time jobs, since Farida reasoned more deeply when the question touched her own life.

qa.q: How might Farida have been affected if the pencil note had stayed?
qa.a: Farida might have been seen and taught as a stage-one thinker, and her stronger reasoning about the curfew could have gone unrecognised.

grounding: A young teacher sees one student reason at different levels over a week and comes to treat the stages as descriptions of reasoning in a moment, not labels on people.

passage:
"Vijay, you're new to tutoring, so let your Preeti Masi tell you about a mistake she nearly made. Sit.
Thirty years ago, in my second year of teaching, I had a student called Harish, nineteen. In class debates he'd say things like, 'Don't cheat, you'll get caught.' I had just read about moral stages, and I wrote in my register: Harish, early stage. Very clever of me.
Then the hostel mess dismissed the cook's helper for taking leftover rice home. Harish stood up in the student meeting and argued that a man feeding his children was not a thief and the rule should change, and he wrote the petition himself.
Same boy. Different day, different question, different reasoning.
I rubbed out my note. The stages help you see where thinking might grow next, Vijay. They are not a ladder for ranking who is good. Harish taught me that, not the book."

qa.q: What did Preeti write in her register about Harish?
qa.a: She wrote: Harish, early stage.

qa.q: How did Preeti feel about her register note once Harish argued for the helper?
qa.a: She felt her label had been hasty, even a bit foolish, which is why she mocks herself with 'very clever of me' and rubbed the note out.

qa.q: What choice at the turning point does Preeti want Vijay to learn from?
qa.a: Rubbing out the label and using stages to see where thinking can grow, instead of ranking students as better or worse people.

qa.q: How might Harish have been treated if Preeti had kept her note?
qa.a: He might have been seen as a shallow thinker in her class, and his fair argument about the helper could have been overlooked.

grounding: A teacher recalls seeing the same student reason at different levels in class and at a hostel meeting, and learning to use stages to see growth, not to rank people.

subtype: Stages are tendencies, not labels on people [Observer]
passage:
Ten minutes into Arnab's evening ethics tutorial, the power went. Twelve phone torches came on, the fan died, and the room at the night college grew hot.
"Keep going, sir?"
"Keep going." He was twenty-two and had planned slides; now he had only a question. "A shopkeeper gives you too much change. Do you return it?"
Kalyani, nineteen, answered from the back. "Return it. He might notice, and then you're in trouble." Arnab caught himself reaching for his notebook to write a stage number beside her name.
Twenty minutes later, sweating in the dark, they argued about whether a factory should cut pay when the staff bus is late. Kalyani spoke again. "Rules should protect workers. If the bus is late for everyone, punishing them isn't fair. It's just easy."
Arnab closed the notebook. Same student, same hot evening, two kinds of reasoning. He had nearly graded a person on one sentence.

qa.q: What did Kalyani say about returning the extra change?
qa.a: She said to return it because he might notice, and then you're in trouble.

qa.q: Why did Arnab close his notebook?
qa.a: He likely felt uneasy and a little ashamed, realising he had nearly graded Kalyani on one sentence when she had just reasoned about fairness in a very different way.

qa.q: What would you advise Arnab to do with the stage idea from now on?
qa.a: Use it to notice how a student's reasoning shifts between questions and where it could grow, not to write a number beside a name.

qa.q: What would change for Kalyani if the power cut had ended the class after the first question?
qa.a: Arnab might have kept a stage number beside her name, and her stronger point about unfair pay cuts would never have been heard.

grounding: A young tutor in a dark, hot classroom sees one student reason at two different levels and drops the idea of labelling her with a stage.
